However, often case list elements represent records, rather individual variables. code: # List holding individual variables z1 <- list(   Height = c(Joe = 6.2, Mary = 5.7, Pete = 6.1),   Weight = c(Joe = 192.2, Mary = 164.3, Pete = 201.7),   Gender = c(Joe = 0, Mary = 1, Pete = 0) )  as.data.frame(z1) # convert z1 to a data frame ##      Height Weight Gender ## Joe     6.2  192.2      0 ## Mary    5.7  164.3      1 ## Pete    6.1  201.7      0 # List holding records (i.e., individual observations) z2 <- list(   Joe = c(Height = 6.2, Weight = 192.2, Gender = 0),   Mary = c(Height = 5.7, Weight = 164.3, Gender = 1),   Pete = c(Height = 6.1, Weight = 201.7, Gender = 0) ) as.data.frame(t(as.data.frame(z2))) ##      Height Weight Gender ## Joe     6.2  192.2      0 ## Mary    5.7  164.3      1 ## Pete    6.1  201.7      0 dmat(z1, rows = FALSE) # treat list elements as columns of a data frame ##      Height Weight Gender ## Joe     6.2  192.2      0 ## Mary    5.7  164.3      1 ## Pete    6.1  201.7      0 dmat(z2) # treat list elements as rows of a data frame ##      Height Weight Gender ## Joe     6.2  192.2      0 ## Mary    5.7  164.3      1 ## Pete    6.1  201.7      0

title: Additional Matrix Functionality
text: ramify R package provides additional matrix functionality. goal make matrix creation manipulation convenient, especially users familiar scientific languages like MATLAB, Octave, Python NumPy.

title: Additional Matrix Functionality
text: Intuitive matrix creation: Create matrices character strings lists using mat(), useful seeing structure matrix code. Block matrices: Easily construct block matrices existing matrix objects using bmat(). Pretty-printing: Display large matrices console compact readable format pprint(). Convenience functions: suite functions familiar MATLAB NumPy users, including eye(), ones(), zeros(), linspace(), meshgrid(), repmat(), .
